JSON: Name: hierarchical_active_inference_abstraction Title: Temporally-hierarchical deep active inference with vector-quantized abstract actions for efficient real-world robot control under uncertainty Short Hypothesis: A temporally-hierarchical world model combined with vector-quantized abstract action representations reduces expected free-energy evaluation time and increases success rates on real-world multi-object manipulation tasks under perceptual and environmental uncertainty, compared to (a) non-hierarchical world models and (b) models without abstract action representations. Related Work: Existing approaches address model-based robot control using learned world models, imitation learning, and active inference. Learned world models enable planning from pixels but struggle with long-horizon dependencies and high-dimensional transition modeling; non-hierarchical latent dynamics often fail to capture slow temporal structure. Deep active inference provides a principled objective (expected free energy) for combining epistemic and extrinsic drives but is computationally intractable when evaluating continuous action sequences online. Action-abstraction methods that compress action sequences into discrete latent codes improve planning tractability, but prior methods either lack explicit temporal hierarchy in environmental dynamics or do not integrate abstract actions with active inference. Diffusion and generative policy methods can produce complex behaviors but require expensive sampling and may not handle long-horizon dependencies efficiently. In summary, current methods are limited by (1) inadequate multi-timescale state representations, (2) high computational cost for planning under active inference, and (3) brittle generalization to action–environment combinations not present in demonstrations. Abstract: Real-world robot control in environments with perceptual and placement uncertainty requires both goal-directed behavior and information-seeking exploration while keeping online planning tractable. We propose a framework that combines a temporally-hierarchical world model with vector-quantized abstract action representations and an abstract world model that predicts future slow state transitions conditioned on abstract actions. The hierarchy separates slow and fast latent dynamics to capture long-term structure, while vector quantization compresses action sequences into a finite set of discrete abstract actions. Action selection is performed by predicting futures for each abstract action via the abstract world model and selecting the action that minimizes expected free energy, enabling joint consideration of epistemic and extrinsic values with low computation. The main contribution is an integrated architecture that makes active inference tractable for real robot manipulation by leveraging temporal abstraction and discrete action encoding. We expect the approach to (i) reduce planning latency, (ii) improve success rates on multi-object manipulation under uncertainty, and (iii) produce exploratory behaviors when uncertainty is high. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Collected teleoperated demonstrations of eight policy patterns combining lid and ball manipulations in a tabletop setup (5 demonstrations per valid pattern, ~100 timesteps per demo, 5 Hz, ~36–72 valid combinations depending on object presence); (2) CALVIN benchmark subset comprising long-horizon language-agnostic visuomotor tasks (eight tasks used for transfer evaluation, ≥128 episodes per task). Baselines: (A) Goal-conditioned diffusion policy (GC-DP) trained to predict fixed-length action sequences; (B) Non-hierarchical variant: identical architecture with a single-level latent dynamics model; (C) No abstract world model (No AWM): hierarchical world and action encoder present but planning uses EFE evaluated directly on reconstructed continuous action sequences. Metrics: task success rate, mean steps-to-completion, expected free energy (EFE) per selected action, EFE computation latency (ms) per planning step, predictive error of slow-state forecasts (MSE), exploration efficiency measured as information gain per executed exploratory action, and statistical significance (paired t-test, p<0.05) over repeated trials. Experimental setup: robot arm with 6-DOF and gripper, RGB camera (64x80 input), actions encoded as absolute joint angles; abstract action codebook sizes K ∈ {4,8,16}, abstract action horizon h ∈ {30,50}, planning horizon τ = t+h, preference precision γ ∈ {1e-4, 1e2} for exploration vs. goal bias. Procedure: (1) Train world, action, and abstract world models jointly from demonstrations; (2) Evaluate online planning on 140 ball-manipulation trials and 24 lid-manipulation trials per configuration; (3) Run CALVIN transfer experiments for 128 episodes per task; (4) Ablations: remove hierarchy, remove AWM, vary codebook size, and vary γ to measure exploration switching; (5) Report mean±std over 5 random seeds and conduct pairwise comparisons against baselines and ablations. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Predictive failure on action–environment combinations not seen in demonstrations can produce incorrect EFE estimates and unsafe robot actions. 2) Fixed-length action sequence encoding limits adaptability to variable-length behaviors and may reduce performance on tasks requiring fine-grained temporal control. 3) Vector-quantized codebook capacity is finite; insufficient codebook size causes underfitting of distinct action primitives, while very large codebooks increase prediction combinatorics. 4) Preference precision (γ) tuning is sensitive and can arbitrarily bias behavior toward exploitation or exploration, limiting autonomous trade-off discovery. 5) Computational bottlenecks remain for extremely large codebook combinations or longer horizons despite reductions; real-time guarantees depend on hardware. 6) Results may not generalize to highly articulated manipulators, deformable-object tasks, or multi-agent settings without additional modeling. 7) Robotic deployment risks include actuator wear, collisions from model errors, and dataset bias from teleoperated demonstrations.
